title: SailPoint Admin Domain 8 questions (8.2 authentication, authorization and federation)
note: Original questions written for Delzar Certification Academy. Not from exam dumps or commercial banks; not affiliated with SailPoint.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes authentication from authorization?
choices: Authentication decides what the user may do; authorization proves who the user is
Authentication applies only to admins; authorization applies only to end users
Authentication happens in the target app; authorization happens at the network edge
Authentication proves who the user is; authorization decides what the user may do
questions.answer: Authentication proves who the user is; authorization decides what the user may do
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity, and authorization uses that identity to decide which actions or resources are allowed. The second option reverses the two terms.

questions.stem: An analyst signs in to the finance portal without problems but receives an access denied message when opening the payroll report. Which process denied the request?
choices: Authorization
Authentication
Federation
Aggregation
questions.answer: Authorization
questions.explanation: The analyst's identity was already verified, so the denial came from the authorization check on the report. Federation and aggregation do not decide individual access to a report.

questions.stem: In a typical access decision, which order do the two processes follow?
choices: Authentication first, then authorization
Authorization first, then authentication
Both run at once and either can be skipped
Authorization only, when a token is present
questions.answer: Authentication first, then authorization
questions.explanation: A system must know who the user is before it can decide what that user may access. Holding a token means authentication already happened.

questions.stem: A user types the wrong password three times and is not allowed into an application. Which process failed?
choices: Authorization
Authentication
Provisioning
Certification
questions.answer: Authentication
questions.explanation: The user could not prove their identity, so authentication failed before any authorization decision. Provisioning and certification manage access, not sign-in.

questions.stem: An identity governance platform such as Identity Security Cloud mainly governs which part of access?
choices: Authorization, by managing which identities hold which access
Authentication, by checking every user's password at each sign-in
Encryption, by issuing keys to every target system
Networking, by routing traffic to each application
questions.answer: Authorization, by managing which identities hold which access
questions.explanation: Identity governance controls who has which roles, access profiles and entitlements, and reviews that access. Sign-in authentication is normally handled by directories and identity providers.

questions.stem: Which of these is an authorization control?
choices: A one-time passcode sent by text to the user's mobile phone
A role that grants read access to a finance file share
A fingerprint scan when the user unlocks a laptop
A PIN prompt when the user inserts a smart card
questions.answer: A role that grants read access to a finance file share
questions.explanation: A role granting read access decides what the user may do, which is authorization. The passcode, fingerprint and PIN all verify identity, which is authentication.

questions.stem: The principle of least privilege is applied mainly through which process?
choices: Authentication, by requiring the longest possible passwords
Federation, by trusting only one identity provider at a time
Authorization, by granting only the access a job requires
Aggregation, by reading accounts from fewer sources each day
questions.answer: Authorization, by granting only the access a job requires
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits what an authenticated user is allowed to do, which is an authorization decision. Strong passwords improve authentication but do not limit access.

questions.stem: An entitlement such as a group membership in a target application is aggregated into the tenant. What does that entitlement represent?
choices: How the account proves its identity to that application
What the account is authorized to do in that application
Which identity provider the application trusts for sign-in
Which password policy the application enforces on users
questions.answer: What the account is authorized to do in that application
questions.explanation: Entitlements are permissions inside an application, so they describe authorization. Sign-in methods and trusted IdPs are authentication settings.

questions.stem: Which combination is true multifactor authentication?
choices: A password plus the answer to a security question
A password plus a code from an authenticator app
A PIN plus a password typed on the same page
Two different passwords entered one after another
questions.answer: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
questions.explanation: MFA needs factors from different categories; a password is something you know and the app code proves something you have. A password and a security question are both knowledge factors.

questions.stem: A user unlocks a laptop with a fingerprint reader. Which authentication factor category is used?
choices: Something you know
Something you have
Somewhere you are
Something you are
questions.answer: Something you are
questions.explanation: Biometrics such as fingerprints are inherence factors, something you are. A password is something you know and a token is something you have.

questions.stem: An employee must insert a smart card to sign in to a workstation. Which factor category does the card itself represent?
choices: Something you have
Something you know
Something you are
Something you do
questions.answer: Something you have
questions.explanation: A smart card is a possession factor. The PIN that often goes with it is a separate knowledge factor, which together make MFA.

questions.stem: Which authentication method BEST resists phishing sites that relay sign-in prompts?
choices: A one-time code sent by text message to the user's phone
A push notification that the user approves on a mobile phone app
A FIDO2 security key that is bound to the website's origin
A security question that the user answers during sign-in
questions.answer: A FIDO2 security key that is bound to the website's origin
questions.explanation: FIDO2 or WebAuthn keys sign a challenge tied to the real site's origin, so a look-alike site cannot reuse the response. Codes and push approvals can be relayed or approved by mistake.

questions.stem: Attackers who have a user's password keep sending push approval requests, hoping the user taps Approve. Which control BEST reduces this risk?
choices: Longer password expiry intervals, so passwords change less often
Disabling account lockout, so that the user is never locked out by mistake
Number matching, where the user enters a code shown on the sign-in screen
Sending a reminder email after each push request is approved
questions.answer: Number matching, where the user enters a code shown on the sign-in screen
questions.explanation: Number matching ties the approval to the sign-in screen the real user is looking at, which defeats push fatigue. Password expiry and lockout changes do not stop repeated pushes.

questions.stem: What does risk-based, or adaptive, authentication do?
choices: Asks for the same factors at every sign-in for every user
Asks for more verification when the sign-in context looks risky
Removes the password prompt once a user signs in from a new device
Grants extra access when a user signs in from the office
questions.answer: Asks for more verification when the sign-in context looks risky
questions.explanation: Adaptive authentication evaluates signals such as location, device and behaviour, and steps up verification when risk is high. It authenticates; it does not grant extra access.

questions.stem: Certificate-based authentication relies on which elements?
choices: A private key held by the user and a certificate the verifier trusts
A shared password that both the user and the verifier store and compare
A security question and answer kept in the user's profile
A session cookie issued by the application after sign-in
questions.answer: A private key held by the user and a certificate the verifier trusts
questions.explanation: The user proves possession of a private key matching a certificate issued by a trusted authority. No shared secret is sent, unlike password authentication.

questions.stem: In an Active Directory domain, Kerberos authenticates users by using what?
choices: Assertions signed by a SAML identity provider
Tickets issued by a key distribution center
Access tokens issued by an OAuth server
Passwords sent in clear text to each server
questions.answer: Tickets issued by a key distribution center
questions.explanation: Kerberos issues tickets from the KDC on the domain controller so users can reach services without resending passwords. SAML assertions and OAuth tokens belong to web federation.

questions.stem: Why are one-time codes sent by text message considered weaker than authenticator apps?
choices: They can be intercepted through SIM swapping or phone number takeover
They can be used only once, so users must ask for a new code each time
They expire after a short time, so users cannot use them while travelling
They require a smartphone, so users with basic phones cannot receive them
questions.answer: They can be intercepted through SIM swapping or phone number takeover
questions.explanation: Attackers can take over a phone number and receive the codes. Single use and expiry are security features, not weaknesses.

questions.stem: What is federation in identity management?
choices: A trust that lets one domain accept identities verified by another domain
A process that copies every user account into each partner's directory
A database that stores the passwords of every user across all organizations
A review in which managers approve each user's access every quarter
questions.answer: A trust that lets one domain accept identities verified by another domain
questions.explanation: Federation lets a service provider rely on an identity provider's authentication through an established trust. It avoids copying accounts or sharing passwords between organizations.

questions.stem: In a federated sign-in, what is the role of the identity provider?
choices: It hosts the application and decides which data the user can see
It authenticates the user and issues an assertion or token about them
It stores the application's data and encrypts it at rest for the user
It provisions entitlements in the application for every new user
questions.answer: It authenticates the user and issues an assertion or token about them
questions.explanation: The IdP verifies the user and sends a signed assertion or token to the service provider. The SP hosts the application and makes its own authorization decisions.

questions.stem: In a federated sign-in, what does the service provider do with the identity provider's assertion?
choices: It forwards the assertion to the user's manager for approval
It stores the assertion as the user's new password hash
It returns the assertion to the IdP to request a password
It validates the assertion and starts a session for the user
questions.answer: It validates the assertion and starts a session for the user
questions.explanation: The SP checks the assertion's signature and contents, then creates a session based on the trusted IdP's statement. The user's password is never shared with the SP.

questions.stem: How does federation differ from single sign-on inside one organization?
choices: Federation extends sign-on trust across separate domains or organizations
Federation requires a separate password for every application used
Federation works only for the applications installed on the local network
Federation removes the need for any identity provider at all
questions.answer: Federation extends sign-on trust across separate domains or organizations
questions.explanation: SSO gives one sign-in for many apps; federation is the trust model that lets that work across security domains, such as with a partner. It still relies on an identity provider.

questions.stem: A partner company's staff need access to your supplier portal. You do not want to manage their passwords. What is the BEST approach?
choices: Create local portal accounts with a shared team password
Copy the partner's password hashes into your directory
Federate the portal with the partner's identity provider
Issue each partner user a personal access token
questions.answer: Federate the portal with the partner's identity provider
questions.explanation: Federation lets the partner authenticate its own users while your portal trusts its assertions. Shared or copied passwords are insecure, and PATs are for API access.

questions.stem: A user opens an application's URL, is redirected to the identity provider to sign in and then returned to the application. What is this flow called?
choices: Identity provider initiated sign-in
Pass-through authentication
Service provider initiated sign-in
Delegated administration
questions.answer: Service provider initiated sign-in
questions.explanation: Starting at the application, which redirects to the IdP, is SP-initiated. IdP-initiated sign-in starts at the IdP's portal and sends an unsolicited assertion to the app.

questions.stem: What is just-in-time provisioning in a federated setup?
choices: Granting temporary admin rights for a short period after a manager approves an access request
Running an aggregation of the identity provider each time a user signs in to an app
Rotating the identity provider's signing certificate just before it expires
Creating the user's account at the service provider from assertion data at first sign-in
questions.answer: Creating the user's account at the service provider from assertion data at first sign-in
questions.explanation: JIT provisioning uses the attributes in the assertion to create the account when the user first arrives. Temporary elevated access is a privileged access feature, not JIT provisioning in federation.

questions.stem: Two organizations set up a SAML federation. What establishes the technical trust between them?
choices: Sharing a list of every user's password between the two directories
Opening the firewall so each side can read the other's user database
Exchanging metadata that includes the IdP's signing certificate
Agreeing on the same password policy for both organizations' users
questions.answer: Exchanging metadata that includes the IdP's signing certificate
questions.explanation: The SP trusts assertions signed with the IdP's certificate, which is exchanged in metadata along with endpoints. No passwords or databases are shared.

questions.stem: Many SaaS apps are federated with the corporate identity provider. What is a key benefit when an employee leaves?
choices: Disabling the IdP account blocks sign-in to every federated app
Each app's local password expires automatically on the same day
Each app deletes its own data about the user immediately
Each app emails the user's manager a list of their files
questions.answer: Disabling the IdP account blocks sign-in to every federated app
questions.explanation: Because the apps rely on the IdP for authentication, disabling one account stops new sign-ins everywhere. Local app accounts and data still need deprovisioning through governance.

questions.stem: Which federation protocol exchanges XML assertions between an identity provider and a service provider?
choices: OpenID Connect
OAuth 2.0
SCIM 2.0
SAML 2.0
questions.answer: SAML 2.0
questions.explanation: SAML 2.0 uses signed XML assertions. OpenID Connect uses JSON Web Tokens, OAuth 2.0 issues access tokens and SCIM is for provisioning.

questions.stem: What does OpenID Connect add on top of OAuth 2.0?
choices: A refresh token that lets the client renew access
An XML assertion signed with the IdP's private key
An ID token that tells the client who the user is
A standard API for creating and deleting accounts
questions.answer: An ID token that tells the client who the user is
questions.explanation: OIDC adds an authentication layer with an ID token about the user. Refresh tokens already exist in OAuth 2.0, XML assertions are SAML, and account APIs are SCIM.

questions.stem: What does OAuth 2.0 primarily provide?
choices: User authentication through XML assertions
Account provisioning through a REST schema
Directory lookups through an LDAP bind
Delegated authorization through access tokens
questions.answer: Delegated authorization through access tokens
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 lets a client get an access token to call an API on behalf of a user or itself. Using it alone for sign-in is why OpenID Connect was created.

questions.stem: In what format is an OpenID Connect ID token issued?
choices: A signed JSON Web Token
A signed XML document
A Kerberos service ticket
A plain-text session cookie
questions.answer: A signed JSON Web Token
questions.explanation: OIDC ID tokens are JWTs signed by the provider, which the client validates. Signed XML documents are SAML assertions.

questions.stem: A team is building a new mobile app and wants users to sign in through the corporate identity provider with a modern, JSON-based protocol. Which protocol fits BEST?
choices: SAML 2.0
OpenID Connect
LDAP
SCIM
questions.answer: OpenID Connect
questions.explanation: OpenID Connect is designed for web and mobile apps and uses JSON tokens. SAML works in browsers but is XML-based and awkward for native mobile apps.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of SCIM?
choices: Authenticating users to web apps through signed XML assertions
Issuing access tokens so that client apps can call protected APIs
Issuing tickets so that domain users can reach network services
Provisioning user accounts between systems through a standard API
questions.answer: Provisioning user accounts between systems through a standard API
questions.explanation: SCIM standardizes account create, update and delete operations between systems. It does not authenticate users, which is the job of SAML, OIDC or Kerberos.

questions.stem: A nightly job must call an API with no user present. Which OAuth 2.0 grant type is designed for this?
choices: Authorization code
Implicit
Client credentials
Device code
questions.answer: Client credentials
questions.explanation: The client credentials grant lets an application authenticate as itself to get a token. Authorization code and device code involve a user signing in.

questions.stem: Why is a SAML assertion digitally signed by the identity provider?
choices: So the service provider can verify it came unaltered from the trusted IdP
So the user can read the assertion's contents in the browser's address bar
So the service provider can decrypt the user's stored password
So the assertion can be reused by any application without checks
questions.answer: So the service provider can verify it came unaltered from the trusted IdP
questions.explanation: The signature proves the assertion's origin and integrity. Hiding the contents from the user needs encryption, which is separate from signing.

questions.stem: A company wants employees to sign in to Identity Security Cloud through its existing corporate identity provider. Which configuration fits BEST?
choices: Set up the tenant as the identity provider for the corporate IdP instead
Create an identity profile on the IdP's sign-in audit log source
Set up SAML single sign-on with the tenant as the service provider
Give every employee a personal access token for the web UI
questions.answer: Set up SAML single sign-on with the tenant as the service provider
questions.explanation: The tenant can act as a SAML service provider that trusts the corporate IdP for authentication. PATs are for API access, not interactive sign-in.

questions.stem: A developer wants a script to call the Identity Security Cloud API with the developer's own permissions. What should the developer create?
choices: A new identity profile
A personal access token
A source service account
A SAML signing certificate
questions.answer: A personal access token
questions.explanation: A personal access token gives a client ID and secret tied to the user, used to get an OAuth access token. Identity profiles and SAML certificates do not grant API access.

questions.stem: A web application must let users sign in and then call the Identity Security Cloud API on their behalf. Which OAuth grant is the BEST fit?
choices: Client credentials
Authorization code
Password
Implicit
questions.answer: Authorization code
questions.explanation: The authorization code grant lets a user sign in and approve the app, which then acts for that user. Client credentials has no user, and implicit and password grants are discouraged.

questions.stem: A user in a profile that uses Directory Connection signs in to the tenant. Which statement about the sign-in is accurate?
choices: The user's AD password is copied into the tenant and checked there on future sign-ins
An external IdP sends the tenant a signed assertion to start the session
The tenant checks the password against the chosen source instead of an external IdP
The user's manager receives an approval request before the sign-in completes
questions.answer: The tenant checks the password against the chosen source instead of an external IdP
questions.explanation: Pass-through authentication verifies the password against the source, such as AD through the VA. With SSO, an external IdP authenticates the user and sends an assertion instead.

questions.stem: An administrator can sign in to the tenant but cannot open the source configuration pages. Which part of access is causing the problem?
choices: Authentication, because the admin's password must be reset first
Federation, because the corporate IdP rejected the admin's SAML assertion
Aggregation, because the admin's account was not yet aggregated
Authorization, because the admin lacks a user level such as Source Admin
questions.answer: Authorization, because the admin lacks a user level such as Source Admin
questions.explanation: The admin already authenticated, so the missing ability comes from user levels, which authorize admin features. Federation and aggregation do not control page access after sign-in.

questions.stem: The tenant uses SAML single sign-on with an external identity provider. Which party verifies the user's password?
choices: The tenant's own password store
The authoritative HR source
The virtual appliance cluster
The external identity provider
questions.answer: The external identity provider
questions.explanation: With SSO the IdP performs authentication and sends an assertion; the tenant as service provider only validates it. Checking a source password is pass-through authentication.

questions.stem: Which users in Identity Security Cloud are always required to use multifactor authentication?
choices: Users who sign in from inside the corporate network
Admins, even when their identity profile has MFA turned off
Users whose lifecycle state is set to pre-hire
Users who belong to a profile with Directory Connection
questions.answer: Admins, even when their identity profile has MFA turned off
questions.explanation: Admins must use MFA regardless of the identity profile setting. Other users follow their profile's settings, and network location does not trigger it.

questions.stem: Which practice BEST protects a personal access token used by an automation script?
choices: Embed its client secret in the script so the token never expires
Share the token with the team so everyone uses the same identity
Email the client secret to the help desk as a backup copy
Keep its secret in a secrets vault and revoke it when unused
questions.answer: Keep its secret in a secrets vault and revoke it when unused
questions.explanation: A PAT carries the owner's permissions, so its secret must be protected and the token deleted when unused. Shared or embedded secrets break accountability and are easily leaked.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a service provider initiated SAML sign-in in order.
items: The user opens the application's URL
The application redirects the user to the identity provider with a request
The identity provider authenticates the user
The identity provider returns a signed assertion through the browser
The application validates the assertion and starts a session
questions.explanation: In SP-initiated SAML the app sends the user to the IdP, which authenticates and returns a signed assertion. The SP validates the signature before creating a session.

questions.stem: Match each standard to its main purpose.

pairs.match: Federated browser sign-in with signed XML assertions
Sign-in with an ID token built on OAuth 2.0
Account provisioning through a standard API

targets_extra: Encrypting data at rest on the virtual appliance
questions.explanation: SAML and OIDC federate sign-in, OAuth authorizes API access, SCIM provisions accounts and Kerberos authenticates domain users with tickets. None of them is a storage encryption standard.

questions.stem: A security team is labelling controls. Which TWO are authorization controls rather than authentication controls?
choices: A role that grants approval rights in the expense system
An entitlement that allows writing to a shared database
A push notification approved on the user's phone
A fingerprint scan at the laptop sign-in screen
A password typed on the identity provider's page
answers: A role that grants approval rights in the expense system
An entitlement that allows writing to a shared database
questions.explanation: Roles and entitlements decide what an identity may do, which is authorization. Push approvals, fingerprints and passwords verify who the user is.
